In which country was House of Plantagenet?
House of Plantagenet: Kingdom of England. The House of Plantagenet was a royal house which originated in the French county of Anjou.
In which country is Battle of Alesia?
Battle of Alesia: France. It was fought by the Roman army of Julius Caesar against a confederation of Gallic tribes united under the leadership of Vercingetorix of the Arverni.

Kingdom of Württemberg: German Empire. The elevation formed part of Napoleon’s broader policy of strengthening allied German rulers in return for political and military support.
Yazidism: Iraq. Yazidism, or Yezidism also known as Sharfadin, is a monotheistic ethnic religion.

Fianna Fáil: Ireland. The party dominated Irish political life for most of the 20th century, and, since its foundation, either it or Fine Gael has led every government.
In which country did the Fyre Festival take place?
Fyre Festival: The Bahamas. Fyre Festival was a failed luxury music festival organized by American businessman Billy McFarland and American rapper Ja Rule.

In which country was the French First Republic?
French First Republic: France. The First Republic lasted until the declaration of the First Empire on 18 May 1804 under Napoléon Bonaparte, although the form of government changed several times.
In which country was Almoravid dynasty?
Almoravid dynasty: Algeria. It established an empire that stretched over the western Maghreb and al-Andalus, starting in the 1050s and lasting until its fall to the Almohads in 1147.
Which of these was an official language of Rattanakosin Kingdom?
Rattanakosin Kingdom (1782–1932): Thai. The Rattanakosin Kingdom, also known as the Kingdom of Siam after 1855, refers to the Siamese kingdom between 1782 and 1932.
Which of these was an official language of the Mali Empire?
Mali Empire: Mande. The Mali Empire was an empire in West Africa from c. 1235 to 1610.

North Sea Empire: Danish. This ephemeral Norse-ruled empire was a thalassocracy, its components only connected by and dependent upon the sea.
Who is credited with discovering Anarchist communism?
Anarchist communism: Peter Kropotkin. Anarchist communism is a far-left political ideology and anarchist school of thought that advocates a form of communism.

This Yemeni religious and political leader has headed a Zaydi Shia rebel movement since 2004, succeeding his brother, the group's founder, after his death in battle, and became a central figure in Yemen's civil war. Who is he?

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi (born 22 May 1979) is a Yemeni politician and religious leader who is the second leader of the Houthis (Ansar Allah), an organization principally made up of Zaydi Shia Muslims, since 2004.
Fill in the blank: “____ (born 16 February 1983) is a Galician publicist and political activist.”
Alejandra Silva (born 16 February 1983) is a Galician publicist and political activist.
Elected in a surprise 2015 upset over the incumbent, who served as Poland's president from 2015 to 2025 after earlier serving in both the national and European parliaments?
Andrzej Duda (born 16 May 1972) is a Polish lawyer and politician who served as the 6th president of Poland from 2015 to 2025.
Blending cultural nationalism with political moderation, this poet and BJP co-founder served as India's PM from 1998 to 2004 after a brief two-week stint in 1996 — who is he?
Atal Bihari Vajpayee (25 December 1924 - 16 August 2018) was an Indian statesman and a poet who served as the prime minister of India, from 1998 to 2004, and previously for two weeks in 1996.

Grandson of the ninth U.S. president and great-grandson of a Founding Father, this Indianapolis attorney and Union veteran unseated incumbent Grover Cleveland to win the White House in 1888 — who was he?
Benjamin Harrison (August 20, 1833 - March 13, 1901) was the 23rd president of the United States, serving from 1889 to 1893.
This Finnish military commander led the Whites during his country's 1918 civil war, later commanded its armed forces through WWII, and became president from 1944 to 1946 — who is he?
Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim (Finland) was a Finnish military commander and statesman.

Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

End of World War II in Europe

This mayor of Istanbul since 2019 was suspended from office in 2025 and held in prison pending legal proceedings he calls politically motivated — who is he?
Ekrem İmamoğlu (born 4 June 1970) is a Turkish politician who has served as the 32nd Mayor of Istanbul since 2019.

Founded in Turkey in 2001 after its predecessor was banned by the Constitutional Court, this Islamist political movement split from the group that also produced the AKP, and regularly accuses Erdoğan of undermining democracy — which movement?
Felicity Party is an Islamist political party in Turkey. It was founded in 2001, and is mainly supported by conservative Muslims in Turkey.
He famously graduated dead last in his West Point class in 1861, yet rose fast as a Civil War cavalry commander before the Indian Wars — which officer was he?
George Armstrong Custer (December 5, 1839 - June 25, 1876) was a United States Army officer and cavalry commander in the American Civil War and the American Indian Wars.

King of Sweden from 1611 to 1632, he is credited with the country's rise as a European power and led its military into the Thirty Years' War, shaping Europe's political and religious balance — name this king?
This Olympian herald of ancient Greek mythology wore winged sandals, guided souls to the afterlife as a psychopomp, and served as messenger between the mortal and divine worlds - name the god?
Hermes (Ancient) is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology considered the herald of the gods.

He joined the King's African Rifles as a cook in 1946, then climbed the ranks until he could seize Uganda's presidency in a 1971 coup — whose eight brutal years in power ended with an ill-fated war on Tanzania?
Idi Amin (30 May 1928 - 16 August 2003) was a Ugandan military officer and politician who seized and held power as the third president of Uganda from 1971 until his overthrow in 1979.
Before three famous Pacific voyages, this navigator first surveyed and mapped the entrance to the St. Lawrence River during the Siege of Quebec — who was he?

James Cook (7 November 1728 - 14 February 1779) was a British Royal Navy officer, explorer, and cartographer who led three voyages of exploration to the Pacific and Southern Oceans between 1768 and 1779.

This Royal Navy explorer survived the Napoleonic Wars and two Arctic expeditions, but vanished on a third attempt at the Northwest Passage when his ships froze fast off King William Island — who was he?
John Franklin (16 April 1786 - 11 June 1847) was a British Royal Navy officer, explorer and colonial administrator.
Though a career scholar and government official during Korea's Goryeo period, this military commander is best remembered for his victories in the Third Goryeo-Khitan War — who was he?
Kang Kamch'an (22 December 948 - 9 September 1031) was a medieval Korean government official and military commander during the early days of the Goryeo period (918-1392).
A rival of Hitler for power, this former Reichswehr leader and Weimar-era chancellor was killed in the 1934 purge known as the Night of the Long Knives — who was he?
Kurt von Schleicher (7 April 1882 - 30 June 1934) was a German military officer and the penultimate chancellor of Germany during the Weimar Republic.
Known as 'the Prudent,' this King of France reigned from 1461 to 1483 after rebelling against his father Charles VII in the failed revolt known as the Praguerie — which monarch is this?
Louis XI (3 July 1423 - 30 August 1483), called the Prudent, was King of France from 1461 to 1483.
Serving as First Mayor of Düsseldorf from 2008 to 2014, this FDP politician went on to chair Germany's Bundestag Defence Committee and later joined the European Parliament — who is she?
Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (ne Jahn; born 10 March 1958) is a German politician of the Free Democratic Party (FDP) who has been serving as a Member of the European Parliament since July 2024.

At Villers-Bocage in June 1944, this German Tiger-tank commander wrecked up to 14 tanks and 15 personnel carriers in a single 15-minute ambush, becoming a postwar 'panzer ace' cult figure — who was he?
Michael Wittmann (22 April 1914 - 8 August 1944) was a German Waffen-SS tank commander during the Second World War.
A former schoolmaster who became India's Defence Minister, this politician served ten terms in his state's legislative assembly and seven in the national Lok Sabha — who is he?
Mulayam Singh Yadav (22 November 1939 - 10 October 2022) was an Indian politician, schoolmaster, lecturer and a socialist figure and the founder of the Samajwadi Party.
Exiled to Onega in 1910 before escaping abroad to meet Lenin and Trotsky, this Bolshevik theorist was active in Soviet government until his 1937 purge — who is he?
Nikolai Bukharin was Soviet revolutionary and politician (1888–1938).
Also called the Old Stone Age, this vast era of human prehistory spans from the earliest known stone tools some 3.3 million years ago to the end of the last ice age — name the period?
Paleolithic is a period in human prehistory distinguished by the original development of stone tools.

In the Hebrew Bible and the Quran, this figure married to an Egyptian guard captain falsely accused Joseph of attempted assault after he rejected her advances, leading to his imprisonment. Who is she?
Potiphar's wife (zoo-), is a figure in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran. The story of Yusuf and Zulaikha is a popular one in Islamic literature.
Hitler called him "the man with the iron heart" — this SS official chaired the Reich Security Main Office and was a principal architect of the Holocaust; who was he?
Reinhard Heydrich (7 March 1904 - 4 June 1942) was a high-ranking SS and police official in Nazi Germany as well as one of the principal architects of the Holocaust.
This royal served as Emir of Kuwait from 2006 until his death in 2020, the fourth son of a previous sheikh who shared part of his name — who was he?
Sabah Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah (16 June 1929 - 29 September 2020) was the Emir of Kuwait from 24 January 2006 until his death in 2020.
After serving as prime minister under Islam Karimov, this leader became his country's second president in 2016 and later chaired the Organization of Turkic States — who is he?
Shavkat Mirziyoyev (born 24 July 1957) is an Uzbek politician who has served as the second president of Uzbekistan since 2016.

A former professor of Mathematical Economics at IIT Delhi, this Indian politician and statistician served as a Cabinet Minister under PM Chandra Shekhar and later chaired a commission on labour standards under PM Narasimha Rao — who is he?
Subramanian Swamy (born 15 September 1939) is an Indian politician, economist and statistician.

This British Labour politician spent 47 of 51 years as an MP and later led the Stop the War Coalition — though for three years he had to be styled The Viscount Stansgate after inheriting his father's title. Who was he?

Tony Benn (3 April 1925 - 14 March 2014), known between 1960 and 1963 as The Viscount Stansgate, was a British Labour Party politician and political activist who served as a Cabinet minister in the 1960s and 1970s.

Likely descended from a group that entered the Roman Empire in 376 and later defeated Roman forces at Adrianople, this Gothic people united under Alaric the First, sacked Rome itself in 410, and founded a kingdom at Toulouse — name this people?
Visigoths were a Gothic people who emerged in the Balkans during late antiquity.

Relocated to San Francisco as a child under a federal urbanization program, this activist joined the Occupation of Alcatraz and became the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation — who was she?
Wilma Mankiller (November 18, 1945 - April 6, 2010) was a Native American activist, social worker, community developer and the first woman elected to serve as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation.
This uprising ended the Qing dynasty's 267-year reign and more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China, ushering in the country's republican era. What is it called?
1911 Revolution: End of Qing dynasty in China. The revolution was the culmination of a decade of agitation, revolts, and uprisings.

Founded in 1912 to oppose oppression of Black South Africans, this liberation movement has governed the country since 1994's first post-apartheid election, when Nelson Mandela became president — which party?
African National Congress: Political party in South Africa.

Amon Göth: Austrian military officer and war criminal (1908–1946)

Antonio Inoki: Japanese wrestler and politician (1943–2022)

Augustus II the Strong: King of Poland, Elector of Saxony and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1670–1733)
In 1575, the combined forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu crushed the Takeda clan's cavalry, effectively securing Nobunaga's unification of Japan — what clash was this?
Battle of Nagashino: 1575 Oda-Tokugawa victory over the Takeda clan.

Cambodian Civil War: 1967–1975 conflict in Cambodia.

Becoming heir to the Habsburg throne after his uncle Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination in 1914, this monarch ruled a central European empire from 1916 until its dissolution in 1918, having secretly sought peace with the Allies during the war — who was he?
Charles I of Austria: Habsburg monarch from 1916 to 1918. Charles succeeded to the thrones in November 1916 following the death of his grand-uncle, Franz Joseph.
The longest-serving leader of the Labour Party, this British statesman was deputy prime minister under Churchill before becoming PM himself in 1945?
Clement Attlee: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1945 to 1951.
This Swedish diplomat became the youngest UN Secretary-General ever at 47, oversaw creation of the UN's first peacekeeping forces in Egypt and the Congo, and died in a 1961 plane crash — who was he?
Dag Hammarskjöld: UN Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961.
Becoming chief minister at just 44 — the second-youngest in his state's history — this Indian politician is now serving his third term leading Maharashtra — who is he?
Devendra Fadnavis: 18th Chief Minister of Maharashtra (2014-2019; since 2024)
This book of Hebrew wisdom literature opens with 'Vanity of vanities! All is futile!', its main body voiced by a speaker called Kohelet — which book of the Bible?
Ecclesiastes: Book of the Hebrew Bible (450–180 BCE)
An Islamic scholar and Sufi who unexpectedly found himself commanding tribal fighters, he held off French colonial forces in Algiers for seventeen years before surrendering in 1847 — who was he?
Emir Abdelkader: Algerian religious and military leader (1808–1883)
Married to Saudi Arabia's king in 1984, this royal spouse is the mother of the crown prince and five other princes — who is she?
Fahda bint Falah Al Hithlain: Third wife of King Salman of Saudi Arabia.
Founded by the Italian saint Francis of Assisi, this Catholic religious family includes the Order of Friars Minor for men and the Order of Saint Clare for nuns — what are its members called?
Franciscans: Group of religious orders within the Catholic Church connected with St. Francis of Assisi.

In January 2021, Reddit's r/wallstreetbets drove the stock of an American video game retailer up nearly 30-fold in a single month, inflicting massive losses on the hedge funds betting against it. What is this market event known as?
GameStop short squeeze: 2021 financial markets event.
The longest-serving Philippine president since Marcos, she first broke ground as the country's first female vice president before leading the nation from 2001 to 2010. Who is she?

Gloria Macapagal Arroyo: President of the Philippines from 2001 to 2010. Estrada was ousted by the Second EDSA Revolution in 2001, and Arroyo was sworn in as president by Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. on January 20.

Ruled by a dynasty once known as the House of Austria, this 1516–1700 European empire commanded territory stretching from the Americas to the Philippines and briefly folded in Portugal — what's this historical era called?
Habsburg Spain: Period of Spanish history (1516–1700)

Often depicted holding twin torches and accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, night, and magic first appears in Hesiod's 'Theogony' and was worshipped in Athens as a protector of the household — who is she?
Hecate: Greek goddess of magic and transitions. The earliest evidence for Hecate's cult comes from Selinunte, in Sicily.
Also known as Brahmanism, this ancient belief system of Indo-Aryan peoples in Punjab and the western Ganges plain (c. 1500-500 BCE) gave rise to today's Hinduism — what was it called?
Historical Vedic religion: 1500–500 BC Indo-Aryan religious practices of northwest India.
Founded in Leipzig in 1984 and now based in Zürich, which organization chronicles the history and statistics of association football despite having no official affiliation with FIFA?
IFFHS: Organisation chronicling the history and records of association football.
This political ideology holds that Islam should shape government and society through the implementation of sharia and pan-Islamic unity — what is it called?

Son of Mary, Queen of Scots, this king took the Scottish throne in infancy in 1567 and united it in personal union with England's in 1603 — though the two kingdoms kept separate parliaments. Who was he?
James VI and I: King of Scotland from 1567 to 1625, King of England and Ireland from 1603.
A Catalan lawyer-turned-club president, he steered his team to a record six trophies in twelve months back in 2009 and returned to the presidency again in 2021 — who is he?

The eldest of nine children born into a family with presidential ambitions, this Navy pilot died in 1944 flying a secret mission called Operation Aphrodite, redirecting his father's hopes to his younger brother — who was he?
Joseph P. Kennedy Jr.: American naval aviator (1915–1944)
Fought between India and Pakistan from May to July 1999 high in the mountains of Ladakh along the Line of Control, this clash was code-named Operation Vijay by India — what is it known as?
Kargil War: 1999 conflict between India and Pakistan. It also marks one of only two instances of conventional warfare between nuclear-armed states (alongside the Sino-Soviet border conflict).
Established in 1832 after the War of Independence, this monarchy survived on and off — including a 1935 restoration — until its final abolition in 1973. What was this Hellenic state called?
Kingdom of Greece: Period of Greek statehood from 1832 to 1923 and 1935 to 1973.
This Colorado congresswoman once ran Shooters Grill in Rifle, where staff were encouraged to carry firearms openly, before her 2020 upset of five-term incumbent Scott Tipton — who is she?

Once president of the Oxford University Liberal Democrats, this British politician later became the shortest-serving prime minister in her country's history, stepping down on her fiftieth day. Who is she?
Liz Truss: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in 2022.
Serving as King Louis XV's official chief mistress from 1745, this Frenchwoman later became the queen's thirteenth lady-in-waiting and a major patron of the arts — who is she?
Madame de Pompadour: Chief mistress of Louis XV (1721–1764)
A chemistry graduate turned barrister, this stateswoman became Britain's first woman prime minister and earned the nickname the 'Iron Lady' — who is she?
Margaret Thatcher: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990.
A civil engineer turned centre-right businessman-politician, he ran Buenos Aires before serving as Argentina's president from 2015 to 2019. Who is he?

Mauricio Macri: President of Argentina from 2015 to 2019. Mauricio Macri ([mawˈɾisjo ˈmakɾi]; born 8 February 1959) is an Argentine businessman and politician who served as President of Argentina from 2015 to 2019.

Serving as the Soviet Union's largely ceremonial head of state from 1919 to 1946 while real power sat with Stalin, this former metalworker had been mayor of Petrograd after the October Revolution — who was he?
Grand Duke Michael Alexandrovich of Russia
Often depicted as King Arthur's sister, this ambiguous enchantress from medieval legend could be portrayed as either a healing fairy or a dangerous sorceress — who is she?

Morgan le Fay: Enchantress in the Arthurian legend. A significant aspect in many of Morgan's medieval and later iterations is the unpredictable duality of her nature, with potential for both good and evil.
After two failed attempts in 1944, this Hindu nationalist activist shot Mahatma Gandhi three times at a Delhi prayer meeting in January 1948 — who was he?
Nathuram Godse: Assassin of Mahatma Gandhi (1910–1949)

Known as "King Father," this royal led Cambodia through French rule, independence, a republic, the Khmer Rouge years and back to monarchy — serving as King, Chief of State and Prime Minister. Who was he?
Of Junker landowner stock, this 'Iron Chancellor' practiced Realpolitik and engineered the unification of Germany, becoming its first chancellor in 1871 — who is he?
Otto von Bismarck: Chancellor of Germany from 1871 to 1890.
Twice imprisoned during a 1920s satyagraha protest, this Indian activist quit the Congress party in 1925 and went on to found the movement behind modern Dravidian politics. Who is he?
Periyar: Indian social activist and politician (1879–1973)

After eight years in UN-funded public health work, this Indian strategist helped re-elect Narendra Modi as Gujarat's chief minister in 2012 before founding his own party ahead of the 2025 Bihar election — who is he?
Prashant Kishor: Indian politician. Prashant Kishor (born 20 March 1977), colloquially known as PK, is an Indian politician, the founder of the Jan Suraaj Party and a former political strategist.

Serving as India's president from 2017 to 2022, he was the first person from Uttar Pradesh and the first member of the Bharatiya Janata Party to hold that office, after serving as Governor of Bihar — who is he?
Ram Nath Kovind: President of India from 2017 to 2022.

Fought from 1921 to 1926, this conflict pitted Spain and later France against Berber guerrillas led by Abd el-Krim in northern Morocco, and saw history's first amphibious landing to use tanks and aircraft — which conflict?
Rif War: 1921–1926 war between Spain and Riffian tribes of Morocco.
From 1904 to 1905, two empires clashed over rival ambitions in Manchuria and Korea, fighting major naval battles in the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan — which war was this?
Russo-Japanese War: 1904–1905 conflict in East Asia.
Renowned in the Book of Genesis for her hospitality and beauty, this matriarch was the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac — who is she?
Sarah: Biblical matriarch. Sarah (originally Sarai) is a biblical matriarch, prophet, and major figure in Abrahamic religions.
In the Book of Revelation, these divine horn blasts — sounded one at a time by angels after the breaking of the final seal — unleash a series of apocalyptic disasters. What are they called?
Seven trumpets: Described in the Book of Revelation. The seven trumpets are sounded by seven angels and the events that follow are described in detail in Revelation 8–11.
Originating from an Old English word meaning 'being truly guilty,' this concept covers immoral or wrongful thoughts, words, or acts across many religions — what is it?
A former professor turned politician, this leader has served in India's upper house of parliament since 2019 and acts as a senior national spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata Party — who is he?
Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught and Strathearn
Younger brother of a U.S. president and an attorney general, he represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 1962 until his death in 2009 — which long-serving senator?
Ted Kennedy: American lawyer and politician (1932–2009)
This retired Royal Navy vice admiral served as an equerry to Queen Elizabeth II before marrying her only daughter in 1992 — who is he?
Timothy Laurence: Retired Royal Navy officer (born 1955)
Explicitly authorized by the Constitution, this independent government agency replaced a Cabinet department in 1971 and holds a legal monopoly on traditional letter delivery — which agency?
United States Postal Service: Independent agency of the U.S. federal government.
Born in Leningrad and working 16 years as a KGB foreign intelligence officer, this politician has served as the de facto Russian leader since 1999 — who is he?
Vladimir Putin: President of Russia (2000–2008; since 2012)
Among Queen Victoria's 42 grandchildren he was the eldest, yet he'd preside over the end of his dynasty's 400-year grip on Prussia when he abdicated in 1918 — which last German Emperor?
Wilhelm II: German Emperor from 1888 to 1918.
Founded by Grigory Yavlinsky and translating to 'Apple' in Russian, this social-liberal party held seats in the State Duma before losing its faction status in 2003 — which party?
Yabloko: Russian political party. The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation of all eight convocations.

The first woman and youngest person ever to hold Slovakia's presidency, this lawyer and environmental activist won the 2016 Goldman Environmental Prize for fighting a toxic landfill in her hometown. Who is she?
Zuzana Čaputová: President of Slovakia from 2019 to 2024.
Who among these was born first?
Saint Valentine (born 175) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (born 1906) is the earliest of the four. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which one below was established earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt is an astronomer. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Hugh Everett III is a mathematician. Hugh Everett III (November 11, 1930 – July 19, 1982) was an American physicist who proposed the relative state interpretation of quantum mechanics.
What is the atomic number of Tin?
Tin is a chemical element; it has the symbol Sn (from Latin stannum) and atomic number 50.
What is the atomic number of Titanium?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
In what year was Archimedes born?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Huntington's disease discovered?
Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Swift (programming language): Apple Inc. Swift compiles to machine code and uses an LLVM-based compiler.
Levofloxacin: Pfizer. Levofloxacin, sold under the brand name Levaquin among others, is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone drug class.
In which country is Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker?
Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker: United States. It has a narrower fuselage and is shorter than the 707.
Who is credited with discovering Roentgenium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Roentgenium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Roentgenium (German: [ʁœntˈɡeːni̯ʊm]) is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Who is credited with discovering 4 Vesta?
4 Vesta: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Who is credited with discovering Lysosome?
Lysosome: Christian de Duve. A lysosome (/ˈlaɪsəˌsoʊm/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.
Sometimes called ajowan caraway or carom, this annual herb in the carrot family produces a seed-like fruit often confused with lovage — what is it?
Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) - also known as ajowan caraway, thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom - is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Despite overseeing Soviet thermonuclear weapons development, this physicist won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize for his activism on human rights and individual freedom — who is he?
Andrei Sakharov (21 May 1921 - 14 December 1989) was a Soviet physicist and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, which he was awarded in 1975 for emphasizing human rights around the world.
Named from the Ancient Greek word for silver, this condition results from too much silver exposure and can leave the skin permanently blue-gray — what is it?
Argyria is a condition caused by excessive exposure to chemical compounds of the element silver, or silver dust.
This large bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists mostly — 70 to 90 percent — of bone. What bird is it?
Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.
Around 2,500 species of this insect family defend themselves by secreting a skin-irritating toxin called cantharidin, often flaunting bold warning colors — which family?
Blister beetle are beetles of the family Meloidae, so called for their defensive secretion of a blistering agent, cantharidin.
The only living group in its tribe, this genus of over 250 fuzzy bees forms small colonies under a single queen — and unlike honeybees, its females can sting again and again — what is it?
Bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' and studies cell-surface sugars called glycans from her professorship at Stanford — who is she?
Carolyn Bertozzi (born October 10, 1966) is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, known for her wide-ranging work spanning both chemistry and biology.
Defined by a hollow dorsal nerve cord, an endostyle, and a post-anal tail at some point in life, this phylum spans vertebrates, tunicates, and lancelets alike — which option fits?
Chordate is a bilaterian animal belonging to the phylum Chordata (kor-).
Though it resembles a barn swallow, this medium-sized bird is actually more closely related to hummingbirds than to any swallow, its resemblance being pure convergent evolution — what bird is it?

Common swift (Apus apus) is a medium-sized bird, superficially similar to the barn swallow or house martin but somewhat larger, though not stemming from those passerine species, being in the order Apodiformes.
Present in the cytoplasm of bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotic cells alike, this dynamic protein-filament network stabilizes tissue and enables cells to migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton is a complex, dynamic network of interlinking protein filaments present in the cytoplasm of all cells, including those of bacteria and archaea.
This Canadian optical physicist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing chirped pulse amplification, a breakthrough in pulsed lasers. Who is she?
Donna Strickland (born May 27, 1959) is a Canadian optical physicist and pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers.
What medical condition, caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, bacteria, or autoimmune disease, refers to inflammation of the brain and can cause confusion, seizures, and memory problems?

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.
Known for filling pillows and blankets as well as lining the wings of birds, what are these soft, complex integumentary structures called?
Feather are epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on both avian (bird) and some non-avian dinosaurs and other archosaurs.
Co-author of 'The Communist Manifesto' and lifelong collaborator with Karl Marx, this German theorist finished the second and third volumes of 'Das Kapital' after his partner's death — who is he?
Friedrich Engels (28 November 1820 - 5 August 1895) was a German philosopher, social and political theorist, journalist, businessman, and revolutionary socialist.
A group 11 noble metal that forms a natural alloy called electrum with silver, this element takes its symbol from the Latin aurum — what is it?
Gold is a chemical element; its chemical symbol is Au (from Latin aurum) and atomic number 79.
Confirming Maxwell's theoretical predictions, this 19th-century German physicist proved that electromagnetic waves actually exist — who is he?

Heinrich Hertz (hurts; 22 February 1857 - 1 January 1894) was a German physicist who first conclusively proved the existence of the electromagnetic waves proposed by James Clerk Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism.
This semi-synthetic opioid, often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, treats severe pain and also suppresses cough — what drug is it?
Hydrocodone is a semi-synthetic opioid used to treat pain and as a cough suppressant.
Many plants stockpile this energy-storing polysaccharide in their roots instead of starch, and doctors still use it as the benchmark substance for testing kidney function — name the fiber?
Inulin are a group of naturally occurring polysaccharides produced by many types of plants, industrially most often extracted from chicory.
This Liverpool-born mathematician roamed from finite groups to knot theory, but is best loved for inventing a famous cellular automaton called the Game of Life — who was he?
John Horton Conway (26 December 1937 - 11 April 2020) was an English mathematician.
This fatal prion disease, once common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, was nicknamed 'laughing sickness' and spread through ritual funerary cannibalism. What is it?
Kuru (disease) was a rare, incurable, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was formerly common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea.
Born in 1880, this Australian therapist and part-time stage actor is remembered for coaching a stammering British monarch — who is he?
Lionel Logue (26 February 1880 - 12 April 1953) was an Australian speech and language therapist and amateur stage actor who helped King George VI manage his stammer.

An engineer and teacher from a poor family who once served as mayor of Tehran, this politician became Iran's sixth president in 2005 and was a fierce proponent of the country's nuclear program — who is he?
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (n Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.
Driven by hormones, this coordinated pair of bodily rhythms — one governing the ovaries, the other the uterine lining — usually runs 21 to 35 days and begins around age 12. What is it called?
Menstrual cycle is a series of natural changes in hormone production and the structures of the uterus and ovaries of the female reproductive system that makes pregnancy possible.
A small terrestrial carnivore of the family Herpestidae that feasts mainly on insects, reptiles, and birds — and turns up as an introduced pest in Hawaii — what creature is it?
Mongoose is a small terrestrial carnivorous mammal belonging to the family Herpestidae.

Sometimes reaching two meters long but often thinner than a millimeter or two wide, these thread-like parasitoid worms turn up in damp puddles, troughs, and swimming pools as adults — what phylum is this?

Nematomorpha (sometimes called Gordiacea, and commonly known as horsehair worms, hairsnakes, or Gordian worms) are a phylum of parasitoid animals similar to yet distinct from nematode worms in morphology, hence the name.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz, and named his improved early radio receiver the 'coherer' — whose key 'syntonic' tuning patents helped birth radio?
Oliver Lodge (12 June 1851 - 22 August 1940) was an English physicist and electrical engineer whose investigations into electromagnetic radiation (EMR) contributed to the development of radio.
This galliform game bird, native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, was once lumped in with pheasants and quail, but DNA suggests it isn't one distinct group at all — which bird is it?
Partridge is a medium-sized galliform bird in any of several genera, with a wide native distribution throughout parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

Sitting at the intersection of textual criticism, literary criticism, history, and linguistics, this scholarly discipline studies language through oral and written historical sources — what is it called?
Philology (from Ancient Greek (philologa) 'love of word') is the study of language in oral and written historical sources.

This category of polymers, most commonly known in the form of PET, is prized for clothing but — unlike some of its naturally occurring plant and insect cousins — rarely biodegrades — what material is it?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.
Ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius believed this oratorical skill could profoundly move even those not present in the room — what is the term for addressing a live audience?
Public speaking is the delivery of a speech to a live audience.

Covering more than 100 conditions like lupus and Sjögren's syndrome and overlapping heavily with immunology, this branch of medicine tackles inflammation in the joints, muscles and bones — what is it called?

Rheumatology (from Ancient Greek (rhema) 'flowing current') is a branch of medicine devoted to the diagnosis and management of disorders of which the common feature is inflammation in the bones, muscles, joints, and internal organs.
This American painter turned inventor co-developed a telegraph system and became the namesake of the dot-dash code that helped make telegraphy commercially viable — who is he?
Samuel Morse (April 27, 1791 - April 2, 1872) was an American inventor and painter.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

Native to China and Vietnam, this invasive planthopper species has spread destructively across the US, feasting on grapevines and stone fruit as well as its preferred invasive host tree — what insect is it?
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a species of planthopper indigenous to parts of China and Vietnam.

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The signs and symptoms depend on the stage it presents: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary.
What culinary herb — the dried aerial parts of plants in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean — is most commonly cultivated in its 'vulgaris' species from Southeast Europe?
Thyme is a culinary herb consisting of the dried aerial parts of some members of the genus Thymus of flowering plants in the mint family Lamiaceae.

This genus of giant theropod dinosaur, whose best-known species takes a Latin name meaning 'king,' roamed an island continent that is now western North America at the very end of the Cretaceous period — name the genus?

Tyrannosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur. The type species Tyrannosaurus rex (rex meaning 'king' in Latin), often shortened to T. rex or colloquially T-Rex, is one of the best represented theropods.
This slender, short-legged predator's genus also includes polecats, stoats, and ferrets, and its smallest species is the tiniest carnivore on Earth — what animal is it?
Weasel are mammals of the genus Mustela of the family Mustelidae.
Discovered in 1807 and named for the Roman goddess of home and hearth, this is thought to be the second-largest asteroid and the only known rocky protoplanet still intact in the belt — which one?
4 Vesta: Second largest main-belt asteroid. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Native to sub-Saharan grasslands and woodlands, this animal is the largest living land species, with the largest recorded specimen standing nearly 13 feet tall at the shoulder — which species is it?
African bush elephant: Species of mammal. Its skin is grey with scanty hairs, and bending cracks which support thermoregulation by retaining water.

This exaggerated immune response occurs when the body mistakes a harmless substance for a threat, triggering histamine release from mast cells and conditions like hay fever or anaphylaxis. What is this reaction called?
Allergy: Immune system response to a substance that most people tolerate well.
This cosmopolitan family of water birds, found on every continent but Antarctica, groups together the ducks, geese, and swans — what is it?
Anatidae: Biological family of water birds. The family has a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on all the world's continents except Antarctica.
Known by common names like greenfly and blackfly, these small sap-sucking insects reproduce via live-born nymphs without males, a trick called telescoping generations — what are they?
Aphid: Superfamily of insects. The group includes the fluffy white woolly aphids.
Originally conceived as the average Earth-Sun distance before its 2012 redefinition, this measure equals about 499 light-seconds and underpins the definition of the parsec — what is it called?
Astronomical unit: Mean distance between Earth and the Sun.
Sitting at the bottom of the forebrain and including the striatum and substantia nigra, this cluster of brain nuclei governs voluntary movement and habit formation — what is it called?
Basal ganglia: Group of subcortical nuclei involved in the motor and reward systems.
Also known as vitamin B7, this B vitamin is found in every living cell and is popularly sold as a supplement; isolated, it's a white needle-like crystal — what is it?
Biotin: Chemical compound and essential nutrient.
This rigid organ not only supports the body and enables movement but also manufactures both red and white blood cells and stores essential minerals — what is it?
Bone: Rigid organs of the skeleton of vertebrates.

Marketed as Wellbutrin, this atypical antidepressant doubles as a stop-smoking aid and stands out for not causing sexual dysfunction or weight gain — what is this norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor?
Bupropion: Medication mainly used for depression and smoking cessation.
Also known as Flinders rose, this perennial shrub with rounded fleshy leaves and white-to-pink flowers is native across circum-Mediterranean countries — what's the plant called?
Marketed as a COX-2 inhibitor, this NSAID treats arthritis pain and menstrual cramps but carries heart attack and stroke risk warnings — which drug?

This antibiotic is used as an eye ointment for conjunctivitis and, when safer options fail, to treat meningitis, plague, cholera, and typhoid — but in newborns it can trigger a dangerous swelling condition called gray baby syndrome — what drug is it?
Chloramphenicol: Antibiotic. Chloramphenicol is an antibiotic useful for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
This French inventor born near Toulouse is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer, but in 1870 he was also among the first to take up the sport of cycling in France — who is it?
Clément Ader: French inventor and engineer (1841–1925)
Better known as "pink eye," this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye can leave a lid stuck shut by morning — what's the medical name?

Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the eye. Conjunctivitis, also known as pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
This species includes honeydew, cantaloupe, and Casaba varieties, and traveled along ancient caravan routes long before its exact origin in the Levant or Egypt was ever confirmed — what fruit is it?
Cucumis melo: Species of plant. Cucumis melo, also known as melon or true melon, is a species of Cucumis that has been developed into many cultivated varieties.
Native to Madagascar and grown ornamentally throughout the tropics, this legume tree is known for its fern-like leaves and a flamboyant summer display of orange-red blossoms — what is it?
Delonix regia: Species of flowering plant in the bean family Fabaceae.
Also nicknamed the French Mastiff, this large, powerfully muscled brachycephalic breed ranks among France's heaviest dogs — which breed?
Dogue de Bordeaux: Dog breed originating in France.
This American astronomer proved that many so-called nebulae were actually separate galaxies, and in 1929 showed that galaxies recede faster the farther away they are — who is he?
Triggered by the parasympathetic nervous system and a rise in nitric oxide, this physiological event leaves an organ firm and engorged — what is it?
Erection: Physiological phenomenon involving the hardening and enlargement of the penis.

Also known as the wisent, this species is the heaviest wild land mammal on its continent — hunted to extinction in the wild by the early 20th century before being restored through captive breeding programs. Which animal?
European bison: Eurasian species of mammal. It is one of two extant species of bison, alongside the American bison.
This genus of about 850 tropical tree, shrub, and vine species is best known for two cultivated fruit-bearing members and serves as a vital food source for wildlife across the tropics — which genus?
Ficus: Genus of flowering plants in the mulberry family Moraceae.
Before becoming Ferrari's Formula One team principal in 2023, this Frenchman co-founded a junior-racing outfit that won back-to-back titles with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg — who is he?
Combining Greek words for 'earth,' 'form,' and 'study,' what field examines how landscapes and seafloor features form and evolve over time?
This plant genus in the mallow family gives us cotton, humanity's primary natural fiber, with its name tracing to an Arabic word for a soft substance — which genus?
Gossypium: Genus of flowering plants in the mallow family Malvaceae.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.
This German-American statistician patented an electromechanical punched-card tabulating machine in 1884, founding a company that would eventually be renamed IBM — who was he?
Herman Hollerith: American statistician and inventor. Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company.

This fatal inherited neurodegenerative disorder, once called a 'chorea,' starts with subtle mood changes before bringing on uncoordinated, dance-like involuntary movements as the basal ganglia degrade — what is it?
Huntington's disease: Inherited neurodegenerative disorder. Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Co-creator of the AlexNet neural network and former chief scientist at OpenAI, this computer scientist has won NeurIPS's Test of Time Award three years running — who is he?
An Indian polymath and pioneer of radio microwave optics, he's also considered the father of Bengali science fiction — and even has a crater on the Moon named for him. Who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose: Physicist, biologist and botanist (1857–1937)
He wrote the first commercial anti-virus software in 1987, then later urged people to uninstall the product bearing his name and twice ran for U.S. president — who was he?
John McAfee: British and American programmer and businessman (1945–2021)
Nicknamed the 'honey bear' though unrelated to actual bears, this nocturnal rainforest mammal is the only member of its genus and a cousin of raccoons and coatis — which arboreal creature?
A hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, this small evergreen tree may have first appeared in northeastern India, and its fruit's juice is about 5–6% citric acid — what is it?
Also called pseudocoma, this condition leaves a fully conscious patient paralyzed except for blinking and vertical eye movement, coined by two neurologists in 1966 — what is it called?
Locked-in syndrome: Condition in which a patient is aware but completely paralysed.
Nicknamed for a Native American tribe, this mulberry-family tree produces a bumpy, orange-like fruit that oozes sticky white latex and is rarely eaten by animals — what's its scientific name?
Maclura pomifera: Plant species in the fig family.
In 2014 this Stanford mathematician became the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal, honored for her work on the geometry of Riemann surfaces — who was she?
Aristotle called it the 'first philosophy' — the branch that probes existence itself, what all things have in common, and how reality is divided into categories of being. Which field is it?
Sold as Remeron, this atypical tetracyclic antidepressant is often chosen when depression comes tangled with anxiety or insomnia — which drug is it?
Mirtazapine: Antidepressant medication. Mirtazapine, sold under the brand name Remeron among others, is an atypical tetracyclic antidepressant, and as such is used primarily to treat depression.

Made of contractile proteins called actin and myosin, this soft tissue exists in three vertebrate forms — skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — and forms during a developmental process called myogenesis — what is it?
Muscle: Important Biological tissue that allows movement.
Named after a German physical chemist, this electrochemistry formula calculates a reaction's reduction potential from temperature, electron count, and reactant concentrations — which relationship?
Nernst equation: Physical law in electrochemistry.

This healthcare profession blends the art and science of caring, focusing on protecting and promoting health, preventing illness, and easing suffering through compassionate, hands-on care — what field is it?
Nursing: Health care profession. Nurses may help coordinate care performed by other providers or act independently as nursing professionals.
Farmed largely around a South African town, this flightless bird is the heaviest bird alive and can sprint 70 km/h — the fastest of any bird on land. What is it?
Ostrich: Genus of largest living birds.
Cultivated across the tropics for its fragrant essential oil, over 90% of this mint-family herb's global oil supply now comes from Indonesia — which plant?
Known on the street as 'angel dust,' this dissociative anesthetic acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and can cause hallucinations and psychosis — what is this drug?
Phencyclidine: Dissociative hallucinogenic drug, mostly used recreationally.
Native to Eurasia and temperate Africa but now naturalized worldwide, this flowering plant shares a common name with a banana-like fruit despite being unrelated to it — which species?
Plantago major: Species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
Covering the front part of the frontal lobe, this brain region orchestrates higher-order thinking including focus, decision-making, and impulse control — what is it?
Prefrontal cortex: Part of the brain responsible for personality, decision-making, and social behavior.
Named by the medieval scholar Gerard of Cremona, this black-looking opening in the eye's iris is round in humans but a vertical slit in cats and a horizontal bar in goats — what is it?
Pupil: Part of an eye. The pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Native to western Europe and known scientifically as Ribes rubrum, which widely cultivated berry has escaped into the wild across many regions?
Redcurrant: Flowering plant species in the family Grossulariaceae.
This British economist, who won the 1991 Nobel and spent decades at the University of Chicago Law School, urged the field to study real-world wealth creation in Adam Smith's spirit — who was he?
Ronald Coase: British economist and Nobel laureate (1910–2013)
First known as a portrait painter, this American inventor helped develop a single-wire telegraph system and lent his name to the dot-and-dash code introduced in 1837 — who is he?
Samuel Morse: American inventor and painter (1791–1872)

Nicknamed the 'last Soviet citizen' for being aboard Mir when the USSR dissolved, this cosmonaut flew six missions and helped connect the first Russian and American modules of a space station — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev: Soviet and Russian cosmonaut (born 1958)
This big cat of the genus Panthera prowls the alpine zones of Central and South Asia at elevations of 3,000 to 4,500 meters, from the Himalayas to southern Siberia — what is it?
Snow leopard: Species of large felid.

First recognized as a distinct breed by the UK Kennel Club in 1935, this purebred originated in 19th-century Birmingham from crosses of bulldogs with various other breeds developed for close combat — what breed is it?
Staffordshire Bull Terrier: British breed of dog.

Blending geodesy, trigonometry, and law, this profession uses tools like theodolites, GNSS receivers, and lidar scanners to fix the exact positions of points on Earth for maps and property boundaries — what is it?
Surveying: Science of determining the positions of points and the distances and angles between them.

Found at the ends of linear chromosomes, this repetitive DNA region works with specialized proteins to prevent the chromosome tip from being mistaken for a damaging double-strand break — what is it called?
Telomere: Region of repetitive nucleotide sequences on chromosomes.
The largest cat of the genus Panthera, this Asian apex predator wears orange fur with mostly vertical black stripes and ranges from snowy Russian forests to tropical Indian jungles — what is it?
Closely related to salmon, these carnivorous freshwater fish spawn in shallow gravel beds of headwater creeks after migrating upstream — what are they called?
Trout: Freshwater fish from subfamily Salmoninae.
Found in Central and South America, only three living species of this blood-feeding, leaf-nosed flying mammal exist, while two extinct relatives once roamed North America — which creature?
Equal to seven days, this standard calendrical period sits between a single day and a month — despite ancient Egyptians preferring a ten-day version, what unit of time is it?
Week: Time unit equal to seven days. The days of the week are often used to set work days, rest days, and holy days.
With atomic number 39, this silvery metal is chemically similar to the lanthanides, never occurs freely in nature, and once gave old CRT televisions their red phosphor glow — which element?
Yttrium: Chemical element with atomic number 39 (Y)
What is the chemical symbol for rhodium?
The symbol for rhodium is Rh. Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
What is the chemical symbol for indium?
The symbol for indium is In. Indium is a chemical element; its symbol is In and its atomic number is 49.

Burt Reynolds: Burton Leon Reynolds Jr. (February 11, 1936 – September 6, 2018) was an American actor.

Jake Paul: Jake Joseph Paul (born January 17, 1997) is an American professional boxer, influencer, and former actor.
In what year was David McCallum born?
David McCallum: David Keith McCallum (19 September 1933 – 25 September 2023) was a Scottish actor and musician.

Diane Kruger (German: [diˈaːnə ˈkʁuːɡɐ], née Heidkrüger; born 15 July 1976) is a German actress.

Steven Spielberg: Steven Allan Spielberg (born December 18, 1946) is an American filmmaker.
In what year did Helen McCrory die?
Helen McCrory: Helen Elizabeth McCrory (17 August 1968 – 16 April 2021) was an English actress.
In what year was Moonfall first released?
Moonfall is a 2022 science fiction disaster film co-written, directed, and produced by Roland Emmerich.
In what year was Dogtooth first released?
